summary: How antennas radiate and receive, SWR, tuning with coils and capacitors, velocity factor, stubs, and the decibel math of line loss and ERP.

blocks.title: How an antenna works
items: Half-wave antenna: a wire half a wavelength long, fed at the center. Wavelength in meters = 300 ÷ MHz.

blocks.title: Along a half-wave antenna
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 122' role='img' aria-label='Along a half-wave antenna, current is maximum at the center and minimum at the open ends, while voltage is maximum at the ends and minimum at the center.'><line x1='20' y1='90' x2='156' y2='90' stroke='#12355b' stroke-width='2.5'/><line x1='164' y1='90' x2='300' y2='90' stroke='#12355b' stroke-width='2.5'/><path d='M20 90 C122 7 198 7 300 90' fill='none' stroke='#1a5fb4' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M20 28 C69 28 118 65 160 90 C202 65 251 28 300 28' fill='none' stroke='#c8452f' stroke-width='2' stroke-dasharray='5 3'/><g font-size='11' font-weight='700'><text x='6' y='16' fill='#c8452f'>Max voltage</text><text x='160' y='16' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1a5fb4'>Max current</text><text x='314' y='16' text-anchor='end' fill='#c8452f'>Max voltage</text></g><g font-size='11' fill='#17202b'><text x='6' y='106' font-weight='700'>Open end</text><text x='6' y='119'>Min current</text><text x='160' y='106' font-weight='700' text-anchor='middle'>Feed point</text><text x='160' y='119' text-anchor='middle'>Min voltage</text><text x='314' y='106' font-weight='700' text-anchor='end'>Open end</text><text x='314' y='119' text-anchor='end'>Min current</text></g></svg>
blocks.caption: Current makes the electro-magnetic field, voltage the electro-static. An excited 1/2 wavelength antenna makes both.

blocks.title: Radiating and receiving
items: Radiation: the changing fields break away as a radio wave.
Radiation resistance: an equivalent resistance that would dissipate the same power the antenna radiates. Knowing it lets you match impedances for maximum power transfer.
Receiving antenna voltage is always proportional to the received field strength.
Vertical 1/4 wave: receives equally from all horizontal directions.

blocks.title: Lines and matching
items: Mismatch: some power reflects, making a standing wave. A detuned antenna coupler can cause it.
SWR, standing wave ratio: highest ÷ lowest voltage on the line. Best is 1:1.
Radiated power = forward − reflected: 30 − 5 = 25 W.
Line current: I = √(P ÷ R). 1,872 W, 52 Ω: √36 = 6 A.
Isolator: passes RF 1 way with very little loss and absorbs it the other way.

blocks.title: Tuning
items: Resonant frequency: set mostly by length. Longer antenna, lower frequency.

blocks.title: Bandwidth, traps
items: Bandwidth: the frequency range over which an antenna performs well.
Loading coils make short mobile antennas resonant on lower bands, but bandwidth decreases.
Trap antenna: parallel LC traps disconnect the outer wire on the higher band, for multiband operation.

blocks.title: Inside the line
items: Velocity factor: wave velocity on the line ÷ velocity of light in a vacuum. Always below 1. Set by the dielectrics.
Nitrogen prevents moisture from entering the line.

blocks.caption: Harmonics: whole-number multiples of the fundamental. The stub absorbs even ones.

items.name: Compare 2 powers
items.means: +3 dB doubles, −3 dB halves, 0 dB is unchanged. Decibels add.

blocks.title: Line loss
items: 6 dB per 100 feet, 200 feet, 100 W: 12 dB is 4 halvings, so about 6 W.
Perfect coax, 7 dB reflected, 5 W in: 1 W out, the exam's answer.

blocks.title: Exam traps
items: The half-power angle is beamwidth, not bandwidth.
Radiation resistance isn't element or feed line loss.
Modulation and power level don't change SWR.
A circulator acts as an isolator only with 1 port terminated.
A 1/2 wave stub would short your main signal.
Nitrogen isn't for skin effect, arcing or SWR.
Net below 0 dB, ERP is below transmitter power.
